That is barely a test at all. The fix is to keep alpha at a level that reflects the cost of a false positive for this deployment (commonly 0.05, lower for higher-stakes decisions) and, if power against a meaningful effect size is too low at that alpha, increase the sample size, which raises power without inflating the false-positive rate.

assessments.prompt: In a hypothesis test comparing a new model's latency to an old model's, which scenario describes a Type II error?
options: The test fails to reject H0, even though the new model truly does have a different average latency.
The test rejects H0 even though the two models truly have identical average latency.
The test correctly fails to reject H0 because the two models truly have identical average latency there.
The test correctly rejects H0 because the new model truly does have a different average latency.
assessments.explanation: A Type II error is a false negative: H1 is true (a real difference exists) but the test fails to reject H0. The “The test rejects H0 even though…” option describes a Type I error (a false positive), the opposite mistake. The “The test correctly fails to reject H0…” and “The test correctly rejects H0…” options both describe correct decisions, not errors: a true negative and a true positive (power), respectively.

assessments.prompt: Holding the true effect size fixed, which change increases a test's statistical power?
options: Switching to a stricter (smaller) alpha, with nothing else changed.
Increasing the sample size in each group.
Increasing the standard deviation (noise) of the underlying measurements.
Decreasing the sample size in each group.
assessments.explanation: More data tightens the sampling distribution of the test statistic under H1, reducing its overlap with the null distribution and increasing the chance a real effect is detected, as this concept's simulation showed, with power climbing from 0.175 at n=20 to 0.985 at n=300. The “Increasing the standard deviation (noise) of the underlying measurements” option is wrong because more noise widens the sampling distribution and reduces power. The “Decreasing the sample size in each group” option is the reverse of the correct lever. The “Switching to a stricter (smaller) alpha…” option is wrong because a smaller alpha shrinks the rejection region, which reduces power (as this concept's alpha sweep shows), not increases it.

assessments.prompt: A team lowers their significance threshold from alpha=0.05 to alpha=0.01 for model-comparison tests, keeping sample size and the true effect fixed, to reduce false positives. What happens to beta (the Type II error rate) as a direct result, all else equal?
options: Beta is unaffected, since it depends only on sample size, not on alpha.
Beta becomes exactly equal to the new alpha value, 0.01.
Beta increases, because shrinking the rejection region makes it harder for a real, fixed-size effect to be detected with the same amount of data.
Beta decreases as well, since a stricter test is better along every dimension, and both kinds of error always move together as alpha changes.
assessments.explanation: This is the alpha/beta tradeoff: for a fixed sample size and true effect, a smaller alpha shrinks the rejection region, which makes a real effect's test statistic less likely to clear the farther-out threshold, raising beta. The “Beta decreases as well, since a stricter…” option ignores that this tradeoff exists at all. The “Beta is unaffected, since it depends only…” option is false -- this concept's alpha sweep, with n fixed, shows power (and therefore beta) changing substantially as alpha changes. The “Beta becomes exactly equal to the new…” option invents a coincidence with no basis; alpha and beta are linked by the tradeoff but are not generally equal.

assessments.prompt: A safety-critical model deployment pipeline and a fast-iterating product experimentation team choose very different values of alpha for their hypothesis tests. Explain, in terms of the real costs of Type I vs. Type II errors, why that difference makes sense, rather than both teams simply using the conventional alpha=0.05.
assessments.modelAnswer:
Alpha and beta aren't abstract settings. They encode how costly a false positive (Type I error) is relative to a false negative (Type II error) in a specific decision, and that cost ratio differs across contexts. In a safety-critical pipeline, wrongly concluding a new model is better and deploying it (a Type I error) can mean shipping something no safer, or worse, where mistakes are expensive, slow to detect, or hard to reverse. That team reasonably chooses a very low alpha (0.01 or smaller) and accepts more Type II error risk, a better model sitting unshipped a little longer while evidence accumulates, because a false 'ship it' is severe and a delayed rollout of a real improvement is comparatively cheap.

A fast-iterating product team evaluating a button color or ranking tweak faces the opposite balance: a wrong 'ship it' call is cheap to detect through monitoring and trivial to revert, while a Type II error, missing a modest real improvement, slows the team's rate of improvement. That team can tolerate a higher alpha (0.10 or more), buying power against modest effects at the price of more false positives, because false positives are cheap there and false negatives are the costlier mistake.

Neither team is being sloppy by deviating from 0.05, a convention and not a law. Each sets the threshold to reflect what a wrong decision costs them.

concepts.title: p-Values and Critical Value Thresholds
concepts.description: A p-value is the probability, computed under the assumption that H0 is true, of seeing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed -- not the probability H0 is true, and not the probability of a false positive -- and it is mathematically just another way of asking whether the observed statistic falls inside the rejection region.
learningObjectives: State the precise definition of a p-value as a conditional probability computed under the assumption that H0 is true.
Explain, with a concrete reason, why a p-value is NOT the probability that H0 is true, and NOT the probability of a Type I error for this specific result.
Demonstrate the mathematical equivalence between 'p < alpha' and 'the test statistic falls inside the rejection region defined by alpha.'
Compute a one-sided and two-sided p-value from a test statistic and its null distribution using scipy.stats.
Identify common real-world sentences that misstate what a p-value means, and correct them.

sections.heading: The Precise Definition, Clause by Clause
sections.body:
A **p-value** is the probability, computed under the assumption that H0 is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed in your sample. Every clause matters, and dropping one is how the definition gets misquoted.

'Computed under the assumption that H0 is true' means the p-value is a **conditional probability**, conditioned on a specific model of the world (the null), not on your data being correct or on any belief about which hypothesis is true. It answers 'if H0 held, how often would data like this arise from sampling noise alone?', not the reversed question 'given this data, how likely is it that H0 holds?' The next section covers that distinction, one of the most consequential mix-ups in applied statistics.

'At least as extreme' depends on sidedness. For a two-sided test, 'extreme' means far from the null value in *either* direction, so the p-value adds up both tails; for a one-sided test, it means far in one direction only, so the p-value comes from a single tail.

```python
from scipy import stats

t_statistic = 2.87
df = 18

# Two-sided p-value: probability of a statistic at least this extreme,
# in EITHER direction, assuming H0 is true
p_two_sided = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t_statistic), df)

# One-sided p-value: probability of a statistic this large or larger,
# in ONE specific direction (H1: the true value is greater than H0's)
p_one_sided = stats.t.sf(t_statistic, df)

print(f"two-sided: {p_two_sided:.4f}")   # 0.0102
print(f"one-sided: {p_one_sided:.4f}")   # 0.0051 -- half
```

`stats.t.sf` (the survival function, 1 - cdf) is used rather than `1 - stats.t.cdf(...)` for numerical precision: for very extreme statistics, `cdf` can round to 1.0 in floating point and zero out a p-value that should be tiny but nonzero, while `sf` computes the tail probability directly. A smaller p-value means the observed data would be rarer under H0, and so is stronger evidence against H0, mirroring 'further into the rejection region' from the previous concepts.

sections.heading: What a p-Value Is Absolutely Not
sections.body:
The most consequential misconception in applied statistics is treating a p-value as the probability that H0 is true (or as one minus the probability that the observed effect is 'real'). It is neither, and the reason is a nameable logical error: confusing a conditional probability with its reverse.

A p-value is P(data this extreme | H0 true). What people often want, and mistakenly believe a p-value gives them, is P(H0 true | data this extreme). These are in general different numbers, and conflating them is the same error as confusing 'the probability a test comes back positive, given that someone has a rare disease' with 'the probability someone has the disease, given that their test came back positive.' The second depends heavily on how rare the disease is (its base rate), information a p-value never uses, because its calculation involves no prior probability that H0 is true. Computing P(H0 true | data) requires Bayes' theorem and a prior for H0, a Bayesian calculation that classical frequentist testing, the framework this module covers, does not perform.

A p-value is also **not** the probability that this specific test result is a Type I error. Alpha is a long-run property of the *testing procedure*: the fraction of the time a procedure like this one would produce a false positive *if run over and over on H0-true data*. It is not a statement about the one dataset in front of you, which either reflects a real effect or doesn't, even though you can't know which. And, as the previous concept's misconception said, a p-value is **not** a measure of effect size or practical importance: a tiny, meaningless true difference can produce a vanishingly small p-value given enough data, as it can a huge test statistic, since a p-value is a monotonic transform of the test statistic.

sections.heading: p < alpha Is the Same Decision as 'Statistic in the Rejection Region'
sections.body:
The p-value approach and the rejection-region approach from earlier in this module are not competing methods that might disagree. They are the same comparison in two equivalent vocabularies. A p-value is a strictly decreasing function of how extreme the observed test statistic is (for a fixed null distribution and sidedness): the more extreme the statistic, the smaller the p-value. That guarantees p < alpha holds exactly when the test statistic falls inside the rejection region defined by the same alpha.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
mismatches = 0
n_checks = 1500

for alpha in [0.10, 0.05, 0.01]:
    for _ in range(500):
        a = rng.normal(0, 1, size=15)
        b = rng.normal(0.3, 1, size=15)
        t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(b, a)
        dfree = len(a) + len(b) - 2
        critical_value = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha / 2, dfree)

        decision_by_p = p_value < alpha
        decision_by_statistic = abs(t_stat) > critical_value
        if decision_by_p != decision_by_statistic:
            mismatches += 1

print(mismatches, "mismatches out of", n_checks)   # 0 mismatches out of 1500
```

Zero mismatches across 1500 generated datasets and three alpha values is not luck. It is a mathematical certainty, and the code is a demonstration, not a test of something that could have come out otherwise. In practice people report p-values rather than critical values because a p-value carries more information: not just whether you'd reject at your alpha, but the alpha at which the decision would flip, so a reader can apply their own threshold to the same number.

sections.heading: Where p-Values Go Wrong in ML Practice
sections.body:
In applied ML work, p-value misuse follows a pattern: a comparison between model A and model B gives p = 0.03, and that number is treated as a settled verdict ('model B is better, case closed') with no effect size, no confidence interval, no mention of how much data went into the estimate. A p-value alone says nothing about how large or reliable the improvement is. A good report pairs the p-value with the estimated difference (in accuracy points, latency milliseconds, conversion rate, whatever the metric is) and ideally a confidence interval around it. The p-value answers 'is this probably not just noise'; the effect size and interval answer 'how big, and how precisely do we know?'

A worse failure mode appears when many comparisons are made against the same validation set during an iterative ML project: twenty hyperparameter configurations, or a dozen feature-engineering variants, each checked against the baseline. Even if every test is computed correctly, reporting only the smallest p-value you found, or treating any config that cleared p < 0.05 as a confirmed win, brings back the chance-driven false positives this framework was built to guard against, spread across many tests instead of one. That failure mode, and the corrections for it, are the subject of the next and final concept in this module.

examples.title: Computing a p-Value Two Equivalent Ways
examples.code:
from scipy import stats

t_statistic = 2.87
df = 18

p_via_cdf = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_statistic), df))
p_via_sf = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t_statistic), df)

print(f"{p_via_cdf:.4f}")   # 0.0102
print(f"{p_via_sf:.4f}")    # 0.0102 -- same answer, more numerically stable
examples.explanation: Both formulas compute the same two-sided p-value, 0.0102, because `stats.t.sf(x, df)` equals `1 - stats.t.cdf(x, df)` mathematically, just computed more stably for the far right tail. For a moderate statistic like 2.87 they agree to four decimal places; the reason to prefer `sf` shows up for very extreme statistics, where `1 - cdf(...)` loses all its precision to floating-point rounding (cdf rounds to 1.0) while `sf` keeps computing the tiny tail probability.

examples.title: The p-Value Decision Matches the Rejection-Region Decision, on Real Data
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

old_latencies = np.array([118, 122, 115, 130, 121, 119, 125, 117, 123, 120])
new_latencies = np.array([110, 108, 115, 112, 109, 111, 107, 114, 110, 113])

alpha = 0.05
t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(old_latencies, new_latencies, equal_var=False)

var1, var2 = old_latencies.var(ddof=1), new_latencies.var(ddof=1)
n1, n2 = len(old_latencies), len(new_latencies)
df = (var1 / n1 + var2 / n2) ** 2 / (
    (var1 / n1) ** 2 / (n1 - 1) + (var2 / n2) ** 2 / (n2 - 1)
)
critical_value = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha / 2, df)

print(f"t_stat={t_stat:.3f}, critical_value={critical_value:.3f}, p_value={p_value:.2e}")
print("via p-value:          ", "Reject H0" if p_value < alpha else "Fail to reject H0")
print("via rejection region: ", "Reject H0" if abs(t_stat) > critical_value else "Fail to reject H0")
# t_stat=6.333, critical_value=2.134, p_value=1.44e-05
# both approaches: Reject H0
examples.explanation: This is the latency dataset from the previous concept's worked example, now checked both ways. t_stat=6.333 clears the critical value of 2.134, and p_value=1.44e-05 is below alpha=0.05; both routes say 'Reject H0' because they are the same comparison. Reporting the p-value rather than just 'Reject H0' also tells a reader the result would still reject at a much stricter alpha, like 0.001, which the bare verdict doesn't carry.

examples.title: A p-Value Misinterpretation Checklist
examples.code:
p_value = 0.03   # result of comparing model B against model A

statements = [
    ("There is a 3% chance H0 (no real difference) is actually true.", False),
    ("If model A and model B truly performed identically, data producing "
     "a difference at least this large would occur about 3% of the time "
     "from sampling noise alone.", True),
    ("There is a 97% chance model B is genuinely better than model A.", False),
    ("This result has a 3% chance of being a Type I error.", False),
    ("The observed data would be fairly unusual under the assumption "
     "that there's no real difference between the models.", True),
]

for statement, is_correct in statements:
    verdict = "CORRECT" if is_correct else "WRONG (common misreading)"
    print(f"[{verdict}] {statement}")
examples.explanation: Running a checklist like this against every p-value you're about to report is a cheap habit that catches most misinterpretations before they reach a slide deck or paper. The two CORRECT statements keep the conditioning direction straight ('if H0 were true, this data would be unusual'), while each WRONG statement flips it into a claim about the probability of H0, or of a Type I error on this result, neither of which a p-value computes.

misconceptions.description: A p-value of 0.03 means there's a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true (or equivalently, a 97% chance the observed effect is real).
misconceptions.clarification: A p-value is P(data this extreme | H0 true), not P(H0 true | data) -- confusing the two is the same logical error as confusing a disease test's accuracy with the chance someone has the disease given a positive result, which also depends on how common the disease is. Getting from a p-value to the probability that H0 is true requires Bayes' theorem and a prior for H0, a Bayesian calculation that a classical p-value never performs.

misconceptions.description: A p-value tells you the probability that this specific significant result is a false positive (a Type I error).
misconceptions.clarification: Alpha is a long-run property of the testing procedure (the fraction of the time a procedure like this would produce a false positive if run repeatedly on H0-true data), not a probability attached to this one dataset. This dataset either does or doesn't reflect a real effect, and a p-value alone can't tell you which or attach a probability to it.

Recall the precise definition: P(data this extreme | H0 true). Is that the same number as P(H0 true | data)?
Think of the disease-testing analogy from this concept. Does a test's known accuracy on sick patients tell you the chance a positive-testing patient is sick?
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 'There is a 3.0% chance the two models truly have the same average latency.' This is wrong because it treats the p-value as P(H0 true), which is not what a p-value measures. A p-value is P(data this extreme | H0 true), a probability computed assuming H0 is true, not P(H0 true | data). exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to compute a two-sided p-value from a t-statistic, but it's returning the wrong number and, in this case, the wrong conclusion. Find the bug and fix it.
exercises.code:
from scipy import stats

def two_sided_p_value(t_statistic, df):
    # Intended to compute a two-sided p-value
    return stats.t.sf(abs(t_statistic), df)

p = two_sided_p_value(t_statistic=1.9, df=18)
print(f"{p:.4f}")
print("Reject H0" if p < 0.05 else "Fail to reject H0")
hints: stats.t.sf(x, df) returns the probability in ONE tail only. Is that the full two-sided p-value, or half of it?
Recall the earlier example in this concept: the two-sided p-value was computed as `2 * stats.t.sf(...)`, not `stats.t.sf(...)` alone.
Compute both the one-tailed value and its double for t=1.9, df=18. Do they fall on the same side of the 0.05 threshold?
exercises.solutionExplanation: `stats.t.sf(abs(t_statistic), df)` returns only the probability in the upper tail beyond abs(t_statistic), which is half of the two-sided p-value, since the symmetric lower tail must be added too; hence the missing `2 *`. For t=1.9 and df=18 the one-tailed value is about 0.0368 (just under 0.05), while the correct two-sided value is about 0.0736 (just over). The missing factor of 2 flips the printed conclusion from 'Reject H0' to the correct 'Fail to reject H0,' though the data and statistic never changed. The code runs fine and returns a plausible-looking number, which is why this bug is dangerous.

assessments.prompt: Which of these is the precise definition of a p-value for an observed test statistic?
options: The probability that H0 is true, given the observed data.
The probability of making a Type I error on this specific test result, computed after the data has been observed.

The probability, assuming H0 is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed.
assessments.explanation: This is the conditional definition: a probability computed assuming H0 holds, describing how likely data this extreme (or more) would be from sampling noise alone. The “The probability that H0 is true, given…” option reverses the conditioning: it describes P(H0 true | data), a different quantity that requires Bayesian reasoning to compute. The “The probability of making a Type I…” option confuses a per-result probability with alpha, a long-run property of the testing procedure. The “The probability that the alternative hypothesis H1 is false” option is effectively a restatement of the “The probability that H0 is true, given…” option's error, just phrased in terms of H1 instead of H0.

assessments.prompt: A model comparison yields p = 0.02. Which statement correctly describes what that number means?
options: 2% of all hypothesis tests like this one turn out to be wrong.
If model A and model B truly had identical performance, a difference at least this large would arise from sampling noise alone only about 2% of the time.
There is a 98% chance model B is genuinely better than model A.
There is a 2% chance the two models actually perform identically.
assessments.explanation: This keeps the conditioning direction intact: the 2% is the probability of the data, assuming H0 is true, not a probability attached to H0 or H1. The “There is a 2% chance the two…” and “There is a 98% chance model B…” options both invert the conditional into a statement about how likely the hypotheses are, which a p-value cannot establish without a prior. The “2% of all hypothesis tests like…” option vaguely gestures at a Type I error rate but misstates it as 'tests like this one turning out wrong' rather than the conditional long-run false-positive rate that alpha, not the p-value, describes.

assessments.prompt: For a fixed alpha, how does the p-value comparison ('is p < alpha?') relate to the rejection-region comparison ('does the test statistic fall inside the region defined by alpha?')?
options: p < alpha holds exactly when the test statistic falls inside the rejection region defined by that same alpha -- they are the same decision, expressed two different ways.
Rejection regions are a fallback only usable when a p-value cannot be computed.
They can disagree, because they use fundamentally different mathematical criteria.
p-values only apply to two-sided tests, and rejection regions only apply to one-sided tests, so the two approaches can disagree about the very same test result and the same alpha.
assessments.explanation: Because a p-value is a strictly decreasing function of how extreme the observed test statistic is, p < alpha and 'statistic inside the rejection region defined by alpha' are equivalent statements about the same comparison, as this concept's simulation showed across 1500 datasets with zero mismatches. The “They can disagree, because they use fundamentally…” option contradicts this mathematical equivalence. The “Rejection regions are a fallback only usable…” and “p-values only apply to two-sided tests…” options both invent restrictions; both approaches apply to one-sided and two-sided tests, and neither is a fallback for the other.

assessments.prompt: A colleague says: 'We got p = 0.04 comparing our new ranking model to the old one, so there's a 96% chance the new model is actually better.' Explain precisely what's wrong with this statement, and state what p = 0.04 actually tells you.
assessments.modelAnswer:
The statement confuses two conditional probabilities that look similar in casual English. A p-value of 0.04 is P(observing a difference at least this large | the new and old models perform identically), computed under the assumption that H0 is true: how surprising this data would be if there were no difference. The colleague's claim, 'a 96% chance the new model is actually better,' asserts something close to P(H1 true | this data), the reverse conditional and a different quantity. Frequentist p-values never compute it; doing so requires Bayes' theorem and a prior probability that the new model is better before seeing any data, which a p-value calculation never uses. It is the same error as concluding, from a diagnostic test's accuracy on people who have a disease, what fraction of positive-testing people have it. That depends on how common the disease is, the kind of prior information missing here.

What p = 0.04 tells you: if the new and old ranking models performed identically, data producing a gap this large or larger would arise from ordinary sampling noise only about 4% of the time. That is evidence against 'no real difference,' but it says nothing about how probable H0 is, how large or important the improvement is, or the probability that this result is a false positive. Alpha describes the procedure's long-run error rate, not this dataset's odds of being wrong.

assessments.prompt: A product manager ran an A/B test, checked the dashboard every day, and stopped as soon as the p-value dipped below 0.05 on day 4, declaring the new design a winner. What is wrong with this, and how should the test be run?
assessments.modelAnswer: Checking repeatedly and stopping at the first p below 0.05 inflates the false positive rate well above 5%, because random fluctuations will cross the threshold at some point if you look often enough. This is optional stopping, or peeking. The p-value is only valid for a test analysed once at a sample size fixed in advance. Run the test properly by choosing a primary metric, the minimum effect worth detecting and the desired power, then computing the required sample size and duration before starting, ideally covering full weekly cycles. Analyse once at the end. If you need to monitor early, use a method designed for it, such as sequential testing with alpha spending or a Bayesian approach with pre-agreed decision rules. Also report the effect size with a confidence interval rather than only a p-value.

concepts.title: Multiple Testing Corrections: Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR
concepts.description: Running many hypothesis tests against the same data inflates the overall chance of at least one false positive far above any single test's alpha, and Bonferroni (controlling the family-wise error rate) and Benjamini-Hochberg (controlling the false discovery rate) are two different, principled corrections, each suited to different ML experimentation scenarios.
learningObjectives: Explain the multiple comparisons problem: why running m independent tests, each at level alpha, inflates the probability of at least one false positive well above alpha.
Derive and compute the family-wise error rate (FWER) for m independent tests as 1 - (1 - alpha)^m, and show how quickly it grows with m.
Apply the Bonferroni correction (testing each hypothesis at alpha/m) and explain both why it controls FWER and why it becomes conservative as m grows.
Apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR), and explain how FDR differs conceptually from FWER.

Connect the multiple-testing problem explicitly to comparing many ML model or hyperparameter variants against a single validation set, and identify why this risk is easy to miss in iterative experimentation.

sections.heading: The Multiple Comparisons Problem
sections.body:
A test run at significance level alpha has, by construction, an alpha probability of a false positive if H0 is true for that test. That is a manageable risk for a single, pre-planned test. It stops being manageable once you run many tests and ask whether *any* of them came back significant. The probability that *at least one* false positive shows up across m independent tests, each at level alpha, with H0 true for all of them, is:

```python
alpha = 0.05
for m in [1, 5, 20, 100]:
    fwer = 1 - (1 - alpha) ** m
    print(f"m={m}: {fwer:.4f}")
# m=1:   0.0500
# m=5:   0.2262
# m=20:  0.6415
# m=100: 0.9941
```

With just 20 independent tests at the seemingly cautious alpha=0.05, there's about a 64% chance at least one comes back 'significant' by pure chance, even if nothing real is going on. At 100 tests it's over 99%. This is the **multiple comparisons problem**, and it applies to a routine ML workflow: evaluating 20 hyperparameter configurations against a shared validation set, checking each one's improvement over a baseline at a naive alpha=0.05, and picking whichever 'won.' Even if none of the 20 is better than the baseline, there's roughly a 64% chance at least one clears the naive bar from validation-set noise. (Real configurations compared against the same baseline and validation set are positively correlated, so the exact figure differs, but the inflation is still large.) Reporting and shipping whichever config looked best is how that noise gets mistaken for a real result. This is the mechanism behind the informally named **'garden of forking paths'** problem: no single test is computed wrong, but trying many paths and reporting the one that looked good brings back the false-positive risk each individual alpha was supposed to keep small.

sections.heading: Controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate: Bonferroni
sections.body:
The **family-wise error rate (FWER)** is the quantity from the previous section: the probability of at least one false positive anywhere across the family of m tests. The **Bonferroni correction** controls FWER with a simple rule: instead of rejecting each hypothesis at the original alpha, reject hypothesis i only if p_i < alpha / m.

```python
import numpy as np

p_values = np.array([0.001, 0.004, 0.009, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045,
                      0.070, 0.090, 0.150, 0.200, 0.280, 0.350, 0.450, 0.600, 0.800])
m = len(p_values)
alpha = 0.05

naive_reject = p_values < alpha
bonferroni_alpha = alpha / m
bonferroni_reject = p_values < bonferroni_alpha

print(f"naive (uncorrected) rejects: {naive_reject.sum()}")    # 6
print(f"Bonferroni-corrected alpha: {bonferroni_alpha:.5f}")   # 0.00333
print(f"Bonferroni rejects: {bonferroni_reject.sum()}")         # 1
```

Why does dividing by m keep FWER at or below alpha? The union bound: the probability that *at least one* of m tests is a false positive is at most the *sum* of each test's false-positive probability. If every test is held to alpha/m, that sum is at most m * (alpha/m) = alpha, whether the tests are independent or correlated in some complicated way. That is a real virtue of Bonferroni: the guarantee needs no assumption about how the tests relate.

That simplicity is also Bonferroni's weakness. As m grows, alpha/m shrinks fast: with 100 tests and alpha=0.05, each test needs p < 0.0005 to survive, a very strict bar. This is the alpha/beta tradeoff from two concepts ago spread across a family of tests: driving FWER down drives beta up for every test in the family, so real effects increasingly fail to survive correction as m grows. Bonferroni is the right tool when a single false positive anywhere in the family would be costly and there's no cheap way to double-check a 'winner' afterward, but it pays for that safety with a sometimes severe loss of power.

sections.heading: Controlling the False Discovery Rate: Benjamini-Hochberg
sections.body:
The **false discovery rate (FDR)** asks a less conservative question than FWER. Rather than bounding the probability of *any* false positive in the family, FDR bounds the *expected proportion* of false positives *among the tests you flagged as significant*, roughly E[false positives / total rejections]. Controlling FDR at level alpha means tolerating some false positives as long as they are a small, controlled fraction of the discoveries you report. That is a more permissive, and often more appropriate, standard when you treat flagged results as a shortlist for further investigation rather than a final verdict.

The **Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure** achieves this with a clean algorithm: sort the m p-values ascending, p_(1) <= p_(2) <= ... <= p_(m), find the *largest* rank k such that p_(k) <= (k/m) * alpha, and reject every hypothesis at rank 1 through k. (The FDR guarantee is proven for independent tests and for certain forms of positive dependence; under arbitrary dependence, the Benjamini-Yekutieli variant divides alpha by the sum of 1/i for i up to m.)

```python
import numpy as np

def benjamini_hochberg(p_values, alpha):
    m = len(p_values)
    order = np.argsort(p_values)
    sorted_p = p_values[order]
    thresholds = (np.arange(1, m + 1) / m) * alpha
    below = sorted_p <= thresholds
    k = 0 if not np.any(below) else np.max(np.where(below)[0]) + 1
    reject_sorted = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
    reject_sorted[:k] = True
    reject = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
    reject[order] = reject_sorted
    return reject, k

reject, k = benjamini_hochberg(p_values, alpha=0.05)
print(f"BH rejects: {reject.sum()}")   # 3 -- more than Bonferroni's 1, fewer than the naive 6
```

On this p-value list BH rejects 3 hypotheses: more than Bonferroni's single rejection, fewer than the naive 6. BH can reject more than Bonferroni and still control a meaningful error rate because of the difference between FWER and FDR. BH doesn't promise that no false positive appears anywhere in the family; it promises that, on average, at most a controlled fraction of what you call 'significant' will be false positives. That is a weaker guarantee, in exchange for more power to catch real effects among many tested hypotheses.

sections.heading: Applying This to Comparing Many Model or Hyperparameter Variants
sections.body:
Read the p-value list as an ML scenario: fifteen hyperparameter configurations, each compared against a baseline on the same validation set, each with a p-value for 'is this configuration's validation metric different from the baseline's.' The naive approach, flagging anything with p < 0.05, calls 6 of the 15 significant. Bonferroni, accounting for the 15 comparisons, calls only 1. Benjamini-Hochberg, controlling a more permissive error notion, calls 3. None of these is the right answer in an absolute sense; which to use depends on what happens next.

If a 'significant' configuration goes straight to production with no further validation, Bonferroni's conservatism is the responsible choice: a false positive there is expensive, and FWER control protects against it. If the flagged configurations are a shortlist headed for an independent confirmatory check (a fresh holdout set, a longer A/B test, a human review), Benjamini-Hochberg's FDR standard is often the better fit. It is built for 'flag candidates for follow-up,' tolerating a controlled fraction of false leads rather than demanding certainty about each one up front.

The deeper fix under either correction is architectural. Where feasible, decide the comparison plan (which configurations, which metric, which correction) *before* looking at results, and reserve a fresh, untouched holdout set for a final confirmatory test on whichever configuration 'won' during exploration. Corrections repair the accounting after the fact; a pre-registered plan and an untouched holdout prevent the problem. In an iterative ML process where a validation set is revisited dozens of times over weeks, that untouched final check is often what stands between a real result and an illusion that is expensive to discover.

examples.title: How Fast the Family-Wise Error Rate Grows
examples.code:
import numpy as np

alpha = 0.05
for m in [1, 5, 20, 100]:
    print(f"m={m}: FWER = {1 - (1 - alpha) ** m:.4f}")

# Confirm by simulation: draw m p-values from Uniform(0,1), which is what
# a correctly computed p-value looks like whenever H0 is true,
# and check how often at least one clears the naive alpha threshold.
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
m, n_trials = 20, 20000
at_least_one = sum(
    np.any(rng.uniform(0, 1, size=m) < alpha) for _ in range(n_trials)
)
print(f"simulated FWER for m=20: {at_least_one / n_trials:.4f}")
# analytic: 0.6415, simulated: ~0.637 -- matches
examples.explanation: When H0 is true (and the test statistic is continuous), a p-value is uniformly distributed between 0 and 1. That is why comparing it to alpha gives a false-positive rate of alpha for a single test, and it is the property this simulation uses: drawing m independent Uniform(0,1) values is equivalent to drawing m p-values from m independent null tests. The simulated rate, about 0.637, is close to the analytic 0.6415, which confirms that the formula describes what happens when 20 independent, individually innocent-looking tests are run against null data.

examples.title: Bonferroni: Simple, Safe, and Conservative
examples.code:
import numpy as np

# p-values from comparing 15 hyperparameter configurations against a baseline
p_values = np.array([0.001, 0.004, 0.009, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045,
                      0.070, 0.090, 0.150, 0.200, 0.280, 0.350, 0.450, 0.600, 0.800])
m = len(p_values)
alpha = 0.05

naive_reject = p_values < alpha
bonferroni_alpha = alpha / m
bonferroni_reject = p_values < bonferroni_alpha

print(f"naive rejects (p < 0.05):        {naive_reject.sum()}")           # 6
print(f"Bonferroni-corrected threshold:  {bonferroni_alpha:.5f}")          # 0.00333
print(f"Bonferroni rejects:              {bonferroni_reject.sum()}")       # 1
examples.explanation: Only the first configuration, with p=0.001, survives the Bonferroni threshold of 0.00333. The other five that looked 'significant' at the naive alpha=0.05 (p=0.004 through p=0.045) fail once the correction accounts for the 15 comparisons actually run. This is the FWER guarantee in action: Bonferroni would rather miss several better configurations than call even one no-better configuration a winner across the family of 15 tests.

examples.title: Benjamini-Hochberg: More Power, a Different Guarantee
examples.code:
import numpy as np

def benjamini_hochberg(p_values, alpha):
    m = len(p_values)
    order = np.argsort(p_values)
    sorted_p = p_values[order]
    thresholds = (np.arange(1, m + 1) / m) * alpha
    below = sorted_p <= thresholds
    k = 0 if not np.any(below) else np.max(np.where(below)[0]) + 1
    reject_sorted = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
    reject_sorted[:k] = True
    reject = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
    reject[order] = reject_sorted
    return reject, k, sorted_p, thresholds

p_values = np.array([0.001, 0.004, 0.009, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045,
                      0.070, 0.090, 0.150, 0.200, 0.280, 0.350, 0.450, 0.600, 0.800])

reject, k, sorted_p, thresholds = benjamini_hochberg(p_values, alpha=0.05)

for rank in range(len(p_values)):
    flag = "reject" if rank < k else "  -- "
    print(f"rank {rank + 1:2d}: p={sorted_p[rank]:.3f}  BH threshold={thresholds[rank]:.5f}  {flag}")

print()
print(f"total BH rejections: {reject.sum()} (Bonferroni gave 1, naive p<0.05 gave 6)")
# BH rejects ranks 1-3 (p = 0.001, 0.004, 0.009) -- 3 total
examples.explanation: The first three sorted p-values (0.001, 0.004, 0.009) each fall below their own rank-scaled BH threshold (0.00333, 0.00667, 0.01), while rank 4's p-value (0.025) exceeds its threshold (0.01333) and every rank after that fails too -- so BH settles on k=3. Rank 2's p-value, 0.004, is larger than Bonferroni's flat threshold of 0.00333, so Bonferroni rejects only rank 1, but it clears BH's rank-scaled threshold of 0.00667. That is the extra power BH buys by controlling a more permissive error notion than FWER.

misconceptions.description: As long as each individual test correctly uses alpha=0.05, the overall set of conclusions from running many such tests is also protected at the 5% error level.
misconceptions.clarification: Alpha=0.05 protects only a single test against a false positive. Running many such tests and looking for any significant result pushes the probability of at least one false positive well above 5%: about 23% for 5 independent tests, 64% for 20, and over 99% for 100, even when H0 is true everywhere. Protecting the whole family of conclusions requires an explicit correction, such as Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg, applied on top of the individual per-test alpha.
misconceptions.fact: Alpha=0.05 protects only a single, individually-run test against a false positive.

misconceptions.description: Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg are just two implementations of the same correction, so it doesn't matter much which one you use.
misconceptions.clarification: They control different quantities: Bonferroni bounds the probability of even a single false positive anywhere in the family (FWER), while Benjamini-Hochberg bounds the expected proportion of false positives among whatever gets flagged as significant (FDR) , a weaker, more permissive guarantee. On identical data, Benjamini-Hochberg routinely flags more hypotheses than Bonferroni because it answers a more forgiving question; which one is appropriate depends on whether a single false positive anywhere would be seriously costly (favoring Bonferroni) or whether the flagged results are a shortlist headed for further confirmatory checking anyway (favoring Benjamini-Hochberg).

exercises.prompt: A team is about to compare 10 hyperparameter configurations against a baseline, each with its own hypothesis test at alpha=0.05, assuming (for this calculation) that none of the 10 configurations is actually any better than the baseline. What does this print, and what does that number represent?
exercises.code:
alpha = 0.05
m = 10   # 10 hyperparameter configurations, each compared to baseline

fwer = 1 - (1 - alpha) ** m
print(round(fwer, 4))
hints: This is the formula for the family-wise error rate across m independent tests, each run at level alpha.
Plug in alpha=0.05 and m=10 directly: 1 - (0.95)^10.
Interpret the result as a probability: if none of the 10 configurations is genuinely better, what's the chance at least one still 'wins' by pure chance?
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 0.4013. This is the family-wise error rate: even if none of the 10 hyperparameter configurations is genuinely any better than the baseline, there's about a 40% chance that at least one of the 10 individual tests, each run at the seemingly cautious alpha=0.05, comes back 'significant' purely from validation-set noise.
exercises.solutionExplanation: 1 - (1 - 0.05)^10 = 1 - 0.95^10 = 1 - 0.5987... = 0.4013. Each of the 10 tests has only a 5% false-positive chance, which feels safe in isolation, but the chance that at least one of 10 independent tests produces a false positive climbs to about 40%, because there are 10 opportunities for chance to produce a good-looking result. That is why picking 'the best of 10 configurations' and reporting its raw, uncorrected p-value against alpha=0.05 badly understates the risk that the 'winner' is noise.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to apply a Bonferroni correction across all the hypothesis tests that were actually run, but a reviewer noticed it under-corrects in a way that lets at least one result through that shouldn't survive. Find the bug and fix it.
exercises.code:
def bonferroni_reject(p_values, alpha=0.05):
    significant = [p for p in p_values if p < alpha]
    correction_factor = len(significant)     # number of tests that already looked significant
    corrected_alpha = alpha / correction_factor
    return [p < corrected_alpha for p in p_values]

p_values = [0.001, 0.004, 0.007, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8]
print(bonferroni_reject(p_values))
hints: The Bonferroni correction divides alpha by the TOTAL number of tests conducted, m. What does `correction_factor` here count instead?
Using only the count of already-significant results as the divisor is circular: it feeds the outcome of the comparison you're correcting into the correction itself.
Fix correction_factor to be len(p_values), the full number of hypotheses tested, whether or not they individually looked significant.
exercises.solutionCode:
def bonferroni_reject(p_values, alpha=0.05):
    correction_factor = len(p_values)   # ALL tests actually conducted, not just the 'winners'
    corrected_alpha = alpha / correction_factor
    return [p < corrected_alpha for p in p_values]

p_values = [0.001, 0.004, 0.007, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8]
print(bonferroni_reject(p_values))
exercises.solutionExplanation: The buggy version counts only the 6 p-values that already cleared the uncorrected alpha=0.05 (0.001, 0.004, 0.007, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045) and divides alpha by 6, giving a threshold of 0.05/6 = 0.00833, which lets p=0.007 through as 'significant.' Bonferroni divides alpha by m, the total number of hypotheses tested (9 here, including the 3 that were never close to significant), giving a stricter threshold of 0.05/9 = 0.00556, under which p=0.007 correctly fails. The bug is circular: using the number of results that already looked significant as the correction factor makes the correction weaker exactly when more false positives are present to correct for.

assessments.prompt: A researcher runs 20 independent hypothesis tests, each at alpha=0.05, and reports that a 64% chance existed of at least one false positive turning up even if H0 were true everywhere. What is this 64% figure called, and how is it computed?
options: The statistical power of the combined set of 20 tests.
The Bonferroni-corrected significance level for the family of 20 tests.
The family-wise error rate (FWER), computed as 1 - (1 - alpha)^m for m independent tests.
The false discovery rate (FDR), computed as alpha times the number of tests, capped at 100 percent.
assessments.explanation: 1 - (1 - 0.05)^20 is approximately 0.6415, matching the family-wise error rate: the probability that at least one false positive appears anywhere across all 20 tests, assuming H0 holds for every one of them. The “The false discovery rate (FDR), computed…” option misnames the quantity and misstates its formula; FDR is a different quantity, and 'alpha times the number of tests' isn't a valid probability once it exceeds 1. The “The statistical power of the combined set…” option confuses this false-positive calculation with power, which is about detecting real effects, not the chance of a spurious one. The “The Bonferroni-corrected significance level for the family…” option describes the corrected alpha/m threshold used to control FWER, not the FWER value itself.

assessments.prompt: Why does the Bonferroni correction guarantee that the family-wise error rate stays at or below alpha, regardless of how the individual tests relate to each other?
options: Because dividing by m always makes each individual test's p-value exactly equal to zero.
Because it requires all m tests to be statistically independent, which mathematically forces FWER down to alpha.
Because it re-runs each test m additional times and only rejects if all m repetitions agree.

Because, by the union bound, the probability of at least one false positive across m tests is at most the sum of each test's individual false-positive probability, and holding each test to alpha/m keeps that sum at or below alpha.
assessments.explanation: The union bound is why Bonferroni works without any assumption about independence or correlation between the tests: summing each test's at-most-alpha/m false-positive probability across m tests gives a total of at most alpha, an upper bound that holds no matter how the tests are related. The “Because it requires all m tests…” option inverts the advantage of Bonferroni, which does NOT require independence. The “Because dividing by m always makes each…” option is a nonsensical mechanism. The “Because it re-runs each test m additional…” option describes a different procedure (repeated replication), not Bonferroni.

assessments.prompt: A team is screening 50 hyperparameter configurations and plans to send any 'significant' ones to a separate, independent confirmatory test on a fresh holdout set before shipping anything. Which multiple-testing correction is the better fit for this initial screening step, and why?
options: Benjamini-Hochberg, because it controls the false discovery rate -- a more permissive guarantee appropriate for a shortlist that will undergo further independent confirmation, and it will flag more real candidates than Bonferroni's stricter FWER control would.
Neither correction is necessary, since the follow-up confirmatory test will catch any mistakes anyway.
Naive, uncorrected alpha=0.05 per test, because the follow-up step makes the multiple comparisons problem irrelevant.
Bonferroni, because family-wise error rate control should always be used regardless of context.
assessments.explanation: Benjamini-Hochberg's FDR control suits this 'flag a shortlist for further review' use case, tolerating a controlled fraction of false leads among the flagged candidates in exchange for catching more real effects than Bonferroni's stricter FWER standard would. The “Bonferroni, because family-wise error rate control should…” option is wrong because Bonferroni's conservatism is best reserved for cases where a false positive is directly costly with no cheap follow-up check, which isn't this scenario. The “Neither correction is necessary, since the follow-up…” and “Naive, uncorrected alpha=0.05 per test…” options both assume the follow-up step removes the need for correction at the screening stage; without one, the screening step is swamped with chance-driven false leads, wasting the confirmatory testing capacity on noise.

assessments.prompt: An ML engineer trains 30 different model variants overnight, checks each one's validation accuracy against the current production model using a separate hypothesis test per variant, and reports the single variant with the smallest p-value as 'the significant winner, p=0.01.' Explain what's wrong with this reporting practice and how it should be corrected.
assessments.modelAnswer:
Running 30 separate tests and reporting only the smallest p-value reintroduces the multiple comparisons problem, even though each test alone looks valid at alpha=0.05. If none of the 30 variants were better than the production model, the chance that at least one test still produces a 'significant' result from validation-set noise is substantial: with m=30 and alpha=0.05 the family-wise error rate is about 78% for independent tests, so a spurious 'winner' is more likely than not. Reporting the smallest p-value out of 30 as if it were the only test run, rather than the survivor of an implicit 30-way search, overstates the evidence for that variant. The p=0.01 headline never accounted for the other 29 chances to produce a false positive.

The fix is to apply an explicit multiple-testing correction across all 30 comparisons made, not just report the smallest raw p-value. If the winning variant ships directly with no further validation, Bonferroni (comparing each p-value to alpha/30) is the conservative, appropriate choice, since a false positive there is costly. If the plan is to shortlist a few promising variants for an independent confirmatory test on fresh data, Benjamini-Hochberg's false discovery rate control is usually the better fit, tolerating a controlled fraction of false leads in a shortlist that will be checked again anyway. Either way, the correction has to cover all 30 tests that were run, not just the one that looked best.
